strengths: Addresses a practical problem: reducing the visual-token cost of video understanding. Combining query-conditioned retrieval, temporal merging, and post-training adaptation is a plausible approach.

Evaluation covers six complementary benchmarks. MARC reports 42.20 average accuracy versus 42.21 for the uncompressed Qwen2.5-VL-3B baseline, while reducing average visual tokens from 2589.93 to 122.69.

The reported memory reduction from 41.63 GB to 11.48 GB is substantial. The VMR and SFT comparisons provide useful preliminary evidence, including an improvement from 40.16 for SFT+VMR to 42.20 for MARC.
weaknesses: The central C-GRPO contribution is not convincingly established. There is no standard-GRPO baseline using identical retrieval, compression, data, and training budget, nor an ablation removing the teacher-dependent bonus. Moreover, if the base reward is binary correctness, the correctness-gated bonus simply rescales successful responses within each group, which cancels under the normalization in Equation 9. The paper must specify the actual reward components and demonstrate that its proposed bonus changes the learning signal.

The optimization formulation contains unresolved technical issues. Equation 10 uses only the clipped importance ratio, omitting the minimum between unclipped and clipped surrogates used in PPO/GRPO; this changes gradients and is neither explained nor justified. The retention ratio is undefined when the teacher reward is zero, and group normalization is undefined for zero-variance rewards. The manuscript does not explain how these cases are handled or precisely how teacher and student rewards are estimated.

Comparisons confound retrieval, compression, and additional training. The main competing compressors do not receive VMR, despite VMR alone improving the full-input baseline from 42.21 to 45.56. The SFT comparison also uses a different dataset and sample count. Matched comparisons with VMR-equipped compressors, ordinary GRPO, and simple low-frame baselines are needed to identify the source of the gains.

The claim of maintaining performance relies heavily on averaging heterogeneous benchmarks. VideoMME drops from 53.55 to 39.44, and VSI-Bench drops from 32.93 to 27.55, while TempCompass rises from 38.05 to 55.34. The manuscript itself attributes the latter gain partly to instruction following. These results support a mixed tradeoff, not broad preservation of video reasoning. There are no repeated runs or uncertainty estimates, and the threshold is selected using the reported evaluation benchmarks without a separate validation protocol.

The compression mechanism is largely heuristic frame averaging rather than a learned compression policy, making the claimed novelty primarily a reward modification and system integration. Its event-preservation claims also exceed the specification: Equation 2 partitions frames into fixed-length windows without showing how event boundaries are respected, and global merging to one frame can collapse the distinctions the retrieval stage seeks to preserve. No ablation isolates event segmentation or the two-stage merging design.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the supplied manuscript. Appendices A and B are repeatedly cited but absent, and an 'Appendix ??' placeholder remains. Essential details are missing, including training hyperparameters, reward definitions and scales, trainable modules, compression-window settings, retrieval configuration, positional handling after merging, and exact training-sample selection. The mixture of public training sources also warrants an explicit benchmark-overlap audit.

Efficiency and deployment claims need tighter qualification. The measured end-to-end speedup is 11.1%, substantially below the emphasized 23.9% LLM-generation improvement. It is unclear whether total latency and peak memory include event detection, embedding extraction, and index construction for previously unseen videos. Evaluation on one benchmark and GPU, with compression demonstrated on one backbone, does not substantiate broad claims about real-time surveillance or autonomous-driving deployment.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: reducing video-language model inference costs through retrieval, temporal merging, and post-training.
Evaluates six benchmarks and reports comparisons with several compression methods at approximately matched visual-token budgets.
Reports substantial efficiency gains: approximately 95% fewer visual tokens and peak GPU memory falling from 41.63 GB to 11.48 GB. MARC also improves over the reported SFT+VMR baseline.
weaknesses: The central claim of preserved performance relies on an aggregate that masks substantial regressions. VideoMME falls from 53.55 to 39.44 and VSI-Bench from 32.93 to 27.55, offset largely by TempCompass gains attributed to instruction following. Against the stronger uncompressed VMR baseline, average accuracy drops from 45.56 to 42.20.

The experiments do not isolate the proposed C-GRPO contribution. Missing controls include ordinary GRPO with identical compressed inputs, C-GRPO without VMR, and compression baselines augmented with VMR. SFT uses a different dataset and sample count, further confounding attribution.

The reward formulation has unresolved technical issues. Equation 6 divides by teacher reward without specifying handling of zero values; Equation 9 similarly omits handling of zero reward variance. Equation 10 clips the importance ratio directly rather than using the standard minimum of clipped and unclipped surrogates, without justification. For binary correctness rewards and a group-shared compression bonus, normalization can cancel the bonus's effect, making the missing ordinary-GRPO comparison especially consequential.

Novelty is insufficiently established beyond combining existing retrieval, cosine-similarity merging, and reward shaping. The cited segmentation model detects shot transitions, which does not establish the claimed detection of semantic events or preservation of complete contextual units. No comparison with fixed windows or simpler retrieval validates this design.

Reproducibility is inadequate in the supplied manuscript: referenced Appendices A and B are absent, and an unresolved 'Appendix ??' remains. Important details about training hyperparameters, reward computation, retrieval configuration, compression placement, and positional handling are missing.

Efficiency evidence is narrow: measurements use one GPU and one benchmark with short answer generation. End-to-end latency improves by 11.1%, whereas the headline 23.9% concerns only LLM generation. Retrieval/indexing cost accounting and its amortization are insufficiently documented, and no accuracy–cost curve establishes the trade-off across compression budgets.

No repeated-run uncertainty is reported, and the threshold is selected using the reported benchmark averages without a described validation protocol. Consequently, small aggregate differences and claims of robust teacher-level retention are not convincingly supported.

strengths: Addresses an important efficiency problem with a plausible combination of query-dependent video retrieval, temporal token merging, and RL post-training.
Reports approximately 95% fewer visual tokens while matching the uncompressed baseline’s mean score across six benchmarks: 42.20 versus 42.21.
Reports substantial GPU memory savings, and the SFT and retrieval ablations provide useful initial evidence: MARC exceeds SFT+VMR by 2.04 mean points.
weaknesses: The central C-GRPO contribution is insufficiently justified. For binary correctness rewards and a shared compression bonus, correctness gating simply rescales rewards, which cancels under group normalization. The paper needs precise reward definitions and a standard-GRPO baseline to establish that teacher-based retention provides a distinct learning signal.

The optimization formulation has unresolved issues: Equation 10 omits the minimum between clipped and unclipped surrogate terms used in PPO/GRPO. Handling zero teacher reward in Equation 6 and zero group variance in Equation 9 is also unspecified.

Comparisons confound retrieval, additional training, and compression. Only MARC receives VMR in the main comparison; there is no matched GRPO baseline, C-GRPO-without-VMR experiment, or direct ablation of the proposed memory-aware merging against ordinary temporal merging.

Matching the aggregate mean does not establish broad performance preservation. VideoMME falls from 53.55 to 39.44 and VSI-Bench from 32.93 to 27.55, offset largely by gains on TempCompass. The stronger uncompressed VMR baseline scores 45.56, versus MARC’s 42.20.

Reproducibility is inadequate. Referenced Appendices A and B are absent from the supplied manuscript. Essential training hyperparameters, reward details, retrieval settings, and baseline adaptation procedures are missing; an unresolved 'Appendix ??' reference remains.

Efficiency evidence is limited to MMVU on one GPU, with only an 11.1% end-to-end latency reduction. The accounting for retrieval indexing and preprocessing is unclear, and no accuracy–latency curves, longer-video scaling experiments, or training-cost analysis support the broad deployment claims.

Novelty and robustness remain insufficiently established: the components largely adapt existing retrieval, merging, and RL techniques; shot-transition detection is not validated as semantic event segmentation; and results lack repeated runs or uncertainty estimates.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: reducing the visual-token cost of video-language models through query-conditioned retrieval, temporal compression, and post-training.

Evaluates on six benchmarks and reports substantial compression: average visual tokens decrease from 2589.93 to 122.69 while the macro-average score remains approximately unchanged (42.21 versus 42.20).
Provides useful hardware measurements: peak GPU memory decreases from 41.63 GB to 11.48 GB, with an 11.1% end-to-end latency reduction in the evaluated setting.
Includes token-budget-matched compression baselines, SFT comparisons, retrieval ablations, and threshold sensitivity experiments. The appendix also acknowledges and discusses failures on long videos.
weaknesses: The central C-GRPO contribution is insufficiently justified. Equations 6–9 do not clearly specify whether compressed reward is computed per completion or per group, the exact base reward, or handling of zero teacher reward and zero reward variance. More fundamentally, with binary correctness rewards and a group-shared compression bonus, correctness gating merely rescales the rewards, which cancels under group standardization. Constant format rewards do not resolve this. The paper needs to establish when its proposed bonus actually changes the learning signal.

The optimization objective in Equation 10 clips the probability ratio directly and omits the minimum between clipped and unclipped advantage-weighted terms used in standard GRPO/PPO. This changes gradient behavior. It is unclear whether this is an intentional algorithmic modification, a notation error, or the implemented objective.

The experiments do not isolate the claimed RL innovation. There is no ordinary GRPO baseline using identical compressed inputs and training data, no removal of the compression reward, and no C-GRPO-without-VMR experiment. Comparisons against training-free methods additionally confound compression with retrieval and post-training. The SFT comparison uses a different dataset and sample count, limiting causal conclusions.

The headline accuracy-preservation claim masks substantial task-specific degradation. VideoMME falls from 53.55 to 39.44 and VSI-Bench from 32.93 to 27.55, offset largely by TempCompass increasing from 38.05 to 55.34. The authors attribute the latter partly to instruction following, so unchanged mean accuracy does not establish preservation of visual reasoning. Relative to the retrieval-enabled uncompressed model, the mean also drops from 45.56 to 42.20.

Novelty beyond the combination of existing components is not convincingly established. Retrieval uses existing segmentation and embedding models, and compression extends similarity-based frame averaging. TransNet V2 detects shot transitions; this does not by itself substantiate claims of semantically complete event segmentation, preserved causal evidence, or human-like memory processing.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the appendices. Important missing specifications include the compression-reward scale, temporal window size, exact reward implementation, teacher freezing or updating, trainable components, training duration, and retrieval embedding aggregation and ordering. The relationship between fixed temporal windows and detected event boundaries is also unclear. Baseline naming and the frame-count column are inconsistent with the stated matched token budgets.

The efficiency evidence is narrow: one backbone, one benchmark, batch size 15, and answer-only generation rather than the reasoning prompt used for accuracy evaluation. Retrieval/index construction and timing boundaries are insufficiently documented. The 23.9% headline improvement concerns the LLM stage; measured end-to-end improvement is 11.1%. These results do not yet support broad claims about real-time deployment.

No repeated runs or uncertainty estimates support the threshold comparison or near-equality of aggregate accuracy. The threshold appears selected using the evaluation benchmarks without a stated held-out validation protocol. Broader compression-budget sweeps and matched uncompressed post-training controls are needed to establish a reliable accuracy–efficiency trade-off.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant problem: reducing video-token costs while maintaining useful video understanding. Combining query-based retrieval, temporal merging, and post-training is practically motivated.

Results span six benchmarks. MARC reports a mean score of 42.20 versus 42.21 for the uncompressed baseline, using approximately 95% fewer visual tokens, and consistently outperforms the reported SFT+VMR baseline.
The paper reports actual memory and latency measurements, includes retrieval and reward-threshold ablations, and acknowledges its substantial long-video performance degradation in Appendix A.4.
weaknesses: The central C-GRPO contribution is not isolated experimentally. There is no ordinary GRPO baseline with identical retrieval, compression, training data, and compute, nor an ablation removing the teacher-dependent reward. SFT uses a different dataset and sample count. Consequently, the results cannot distinguish teacher-guided compression benefits from ordinary RL or improved instruction following.

The reward formulation raises an unresolved technical concern. For binary correctness rewards with constant format rewards within a group, the correctness-gated compression bonus simply rescales the correct/incorrect reward gap; group standardization in Equation 9 cancels that rescaling. The paper needs to specify the actual reward components and demonstrate when the teacher-dependent term changes the advantages. Handling of zero teacher reward and zero within-group reward variance is also unspecified.

Equation 10 is not the standard PPO/GRPO clipped surrogate: it omits the minimum between the unclipped and clipped advantage-weighted ratios. This changes optimization behavior. The manuscript does not establish whether this is a notation error or the implemented objective, leaving the central training method insufficiently specified.

The headline performance-retention claim relies on averaging heterogeneous outcomes. VideoMME drops from 53.55 to 39.44 and VSI-Bench from 32.93 to 27.55, offset largely by TempCompass improving from 38.05 to 55.34, which the authors attribute to instruction following. Moreover, the retrieval-equipped uncompressed baseline scores 45.56, substantially above MARC's 42.20. These results support a useful tradeoff, but not broad preservation of teacher-level reasoning.

Comparisons do not adequately establish the proposed mechanism's advantage. Only MARC receives retrieval in Table 1, and competing compressors are not evaluated with matched post-training. Missing controls include VMR plus the proposed merger without training, ordinary averaging or frame selection, and event-based versus fixed-window segmentation. The memory-aware design is therefore difficult to separate from familiar retrieval and merging components.

Efficiency evidence is narrow: one benchmark, one batch size, and an answer-only prompt that differs from the accuracy evaluation. End-to-end latency improves by 11.1%, whereas the prominently advertised 23.9% refers only to LLM latency. The inclusion and amortization of segmentation, embedding, and indexing costs need clarification, and accuracy under the timing configuration is not reported.

Reproducibility and robustness remain insufficient. Important details include the reward scale alpha, exact reward computation, teacher update policy, compression-window settings, training duration, and which parameters are trained. No repeated-run uncertainty is supplied for the threshold ablation, and no separate validation procedure is described for selecting tau. The claimed semantic-event preservation also exceeds what is demonstrated by using a shot-transition detector.

strengths: Addresses an important practical problem: reducing video-token costs while preserving downstream accuracy. The retrieve-then-compress pipeline is intuitive and potentially useful.

Experiments cover six benchmarks and report substantial savings: approximately 95% fewer visual tokens and 72% lower peak GPU memory, with macro-average accuracy close to the uncompressed baseline (42.20 versus 42.21).
Includes comparisons with several compression methods, SFT controls, retrieval ablations, threshold sensitivity, and measured latency. Appendix A.4 candidly discusses failures on long videos.
weaknesses: The central C-GRPO contribution is not established. There is no standard-GRPO baseline using the same data, retrieval, and compression, nor an ablation removing the compression reward. Consequently, the improvements cannot be attributed to the proposed teacher-dependent reward rather than ordinary RL post-training. SFT comparisons also use different training data and supervision.

The reward formulation raises a substantive concern. Equations 7–9 introduce a correctness-gated bonus followed by within-group normalization. When the base reward is binary correctness and the bonus is shared across correct responses, this merely rescales rewards and cancels under normalization. Additional format or graded rewards could change this, but their definitions and weights are not specified sufficiently to establish a distinct learning signal. Matching scalar reward levels also does not by itself demonstrate transfer of teacher reasoning.

The optimization specification is incomplete and potentially incorrect. Equation 10 clips the likelihood ratio directly rather than using the standard PPO/GRPO minimum of clipped and unclipped surrogate terms. Handling of zero teacher reward and zero reward variance is unspecified. Important reproducibility details, including the compression-reward scale, training duration, trainable components, memory-window size, and precise retrieval configuration, are missing.

The headline accuracy-retention claim obscures heterogeneous outcomes. VideoMME falls from 53.55 to 39.44 and VSI-Bench from 32.93 to 27.55; these losses are offset largely by the TempCompass improvement. Moreover, the retrieval-equipped uncompressed baseline scores 45.56, versus MARC's 42.20. Thus, compression does incur a meaningful loss against the more closely matched baseline. No uncertainty estimates support claims of equivalence.

Comparisons do not adequately isolate the method's advantages. Only MARC receives retrieval in the main comparison, and the compression baselines lack matched post-training. Missing controls include retrieval plus compression without training, C-GRPO without retrieval, and simpler merging or frame-selection alternatives. The unusually low InternVL3.5-2B results, including 4.26 on VideoMME, also warrant an implementation and answer-parsing audit.

Efficiency and generality claims exceed the demonstrated scope. The reported end-to-end latency improvement is 11.1%, while 23.9% applies only to LLM generation. Measurements cover one benchmark, hardware configuration, and batch size, using a different output protocol from accuracy evaluation; retrieval/indexing cost accounting is insufficiently explicit. MARC is trained on only one backbone, and neither real-time deployment nor the claimed benefits for autonomous driving and surveillance are evaluated.
